title: Designing Gmail
article: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/design-gmail.md

facts.text: The system must get a user's email into the recipient's mailbox, where the recipient's client can fetch it: Alice sends from her client, and the Gmail server stores the mail and makes it available to Bob.
SMTP's objective is to transfer mail reliably and efficiently, and email favors reliability over speed so it copes with unreliable network links and busy servers.

RFC 5321 sets minimums: message content of at least 64K octets, 100 buffered recipients, local parts up to 64 octets and domains up to 255. Providers cap attachments, typically at 25MB or less in the early 2010s.
SMTP is the protocol between client and server and between mail servers, but it only delivers; the recipient's client fetches mail from the mailbox with IMAP or POP.

A mail object is an envelope, with the error-return address and recipients, plus content of header and body. Delivery follows the envelope, so To can differ from the delivery list, and Bcc lives only in the envelope.

Every message has a globally unique Message-ID, and replies name the parent in In-Reply-To and References, which lets a client rebuild conversation threads. Headers follow RFC 5322, and non-ASCII text and attachments use MIME.

The server keeps each mailbox: messages with strictly ascending UIDs and a UIDVALIDITY value, per-message flags such as \Seen and \Deleted, and folders. This server-held state costs far more per mailbox than POP.
Alice's client submits the message by SMTP to her mail server, on port 587 or 465 with authentication, and that server hands it to its mail transfer agent.
The sending MTA asks DNS for the MX records of the recipient's domain and tries the lowest preference first, randomizing among equals. For a Gmail address the answer is Gmail's SMTP server.

The MTA connects to the receiving server on port 25 and runs MAIL, RCPT and DATA, sending one copy for all recipients there. After the final 250 the receiver owns the message and must deliver it or report failure.
A mail delivery agent saves the accepted message in the recipient's mailbox format, so the Gmail server holds the mail until Bob's client asks for it.

When Bob logs in, his client fetches new mail through the IMAP/POP server. IMAP leaves messages on the server so several clients share a mailbox, POP downloads and deletes, and IMAP IDLE pushes new-mail notices instead of polling.

IMAP lets the server search so clients need not download every message, and fetch single MIME parts such as text without attachments. Searching massive mailboxes can overload the server unless storage, indexing and search are carefully built.

About 85% of email was estimated to be spam in 2021, so incoming mail is filtered by content, DNS blocklists, greylisting, Bayesian or learned models and sender authentication. Mail sent to a spam folder gives the sender no notice.

Attachments travel as MIME parts: original SMTP carries only 7-bit ASCII, so binary files are base64-encoded into a multipart message, and the size the transport sees can differ from what the user sees.

Mail that cannot be sent is queued and retried, at least 30 minutes apart, for at least 4-5 days. Several MX servers keep a domain accepting mail if one fails, and undeliverable mail is bounced with a null return path.

notes: thin: no source gives Gmail's scale or traffic estimates, mailbox storage layout, search indexing design, or an API; the answer is built from the SMTP, IMAP, POP, MX and message-format standards and the Wikipedia pages on email and spam.

sources.title: RFC 9051: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) - Version 4rev2

title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
article: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol

definition.text: SMTP is the Internet standard protocol that mail servers and clients use to transmit electronic mail.

facts.text: SMTP is a connection-oriented, text-based protocol: a sender issues command strings and a receiver replies, over a reliable ordered data stream, typically a TCP connection.
SMTP is a delivery protocol only: mail is pushed to the next-hop server as it arrives and routed by destination server, not by individual user. POP and IMAP handle retrieval.
A mail transaction is three command/reply steps: MAIL gives the return address, RCPT names one recipient (repeated per recipient), and DATA carries the header, a blank line and the body.
The server replies twice to DATA, once to say it is ready and once after the end-of-data marker to accept or reject the whole message. Replies are 2xx positive, 4xx transient or 5xx permanent.
Servers talk to each other on TCP port 25, while clients submit mail to a submission server on port 465 or 587, which requires SMTP authentication.
Fully capable servers keep queues and retry transient failures. A server that accepts a message takes responsibility for delivering it or reporting the failure.
SMTP defines message transport, the envelope, not content: RFC 5321 defines SMTP and RFC 5322 defines the message header and body.

Original SMTP could not authenticate senders, so spoofing is possible. Modern servers require client authentication and use SPF, DKIM, DMARC, DNSBLs and greylisting to reject or quarantine suspicious mail.

title: Mail agents and relays
article: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol#Mail processing model

definition.text: Mail passes through user agents, submission agents, transfer agents and delivery agents, each with its own role.

facts.text: A mail user agent submits mail to a mail submission agent, which hands it to a mail transfer agent. These two agents are often the same software started with different options.
The boundary MTA looks up the MX record for the recipient's domain and connects to the target MTA. Transfer is one connection between two MTAs or a series of hops through intermediaries.
A receiving server may be the final destination, a relay that stores and forwards, or a gateway that forwards using a protocol other than SMTP.
A relay passes on the message data without modification except for adding trace information, whereas a gateway may need to transform the message because the two transport environments differ.
Counting the Received header fields in a message is an effective way to detect mail loops; servers using it should use a large rejection threshold, normally at least 100 entries.
The final hop hands the message to a mail delivery agent, which saves it in the mailbox format or forwards it by SMTP or LMTP. Clients then retrieve mail with IMAP or POP.
A relay is usually the target of an MX record. It may accept or decline relaying as it would for a local user, becomes an SMTP client if it accepts, and returns 550 if policy forbids relaying.
Clients that cannot queue mail for retry, such as those paired with POP or IMAP, send everything to a single submission server; a message submission protocol is superseding such arrangements.

title: SMTP extensions
article: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol#SMTP Extensions

definition.text: The SMTP service-extension model lets a client and server agree to use features beyond the original protocol.

facts.text: A client opens with EHLO instead of HELO, and the server answers 250 with a multi-line list of keywords for the extensions it supports. Clients fall back to HELO only when EHLO is not supported.
The IANA keeps a registry of extensions. Common keywords include 8BITMIME, AUTH, PIPELINING, SIZE, STARTTLS and SMTPUTF8.
SIZE lets a server declare the largest message it accepts, so clients avoid sending oversized messages that would be rejected after using up network resources.
Original SMTP carries only one body of ASCII text, so binary data had to be encoded as text. 8BITMIME allows octets outside seven-bit ASCII, encoded as MIME parts, typically Base64.

notes: excluded: protocol detail beyond what the Gmail design needs

title: SMTP security
article: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol#SMTP Extensions > Security extensions

definition.text: SMTP security covers authenticating clients, encrypting server-to-server connections and declaring a domain's TLS policy.

facts.text: SMTP-AUTH makes the client log in to the mail server while sending, letting legitimate users relay mail and denying relay to spammers.
SMTP-AUTH does not guarantee the authenticity of the envelope sender or the From header, so spoofing is still possible unless the server limits from-addresses to those the authenticated user may use.
STARTTLS lets a server advertise TLS and a client upgrade the connection. It is opportunistic: the server gains no security unless the client chooses to upgrade.
STARTTLS resists only passive observation, since negotiation is in plain text and an active attacker can strip the STARTTLS commands, a downgrade known as STRIPTLS.
MTA-STS lets a domain declare in a policy file and DNS TXT record that it supports secure channels; senders cache it and never use insecure channels until it expires.
DANE for SMTP lets operators publish a hash of their TLS certificate in DNS secured by DNSSEC, which reduces the chance of unencrypted delivery.
RFC 8314 declared plain text obsolete and recommends always using TLS for mail submission and access, adding ports with implicit TLS.
SMTP cannot authenticate mail or check integrity at the transport level; real mail security lies in end-to-end methods on the message body, such as digital signatures.

title: Internet Message Access Protocol
article: Internet Message Access Protocol

definition.text: IMAP is an Internet standard protocol that email clients use to retrieve and manage messages on a mail server over a TCP/IP connection.

facts.text: IMAP was designed for complete management of a mailbox by multiple clients, so clients generally leave messages on the server until the user deletes them. It makes remote mailboxes work like local folders.
The server holds the mailbox structure: content, folders and per-message state. Local copies are a temporary cache, and this makes IMAP need far more server resources and cost per mailbox than POP.
Clients often stay connected and download message content on demand, which can give faster response for large mailboxes. The server reports new messages and changes made by other clients.

Flags such as read, replied to or deleted are stored on the server, so different clients see each other's changes. IMAP also supports client-defined keywords and creating, renaming and deleting mailboxes.

IMAP can ask the server to search by criteria so clients need not download every message, but searching massive mailboxes can burden the server unless its storage, indexing and search are carefully built.
Clients can fetch individual MIME parts or portions of a message, such as the text without its attachments, or stream content as it is fetched.
IMAP IDLE lets the server notify connected clients of mailbox changes such as new mail, but clients must keep a TCP connection open to be notified.
An IMAP server listens on port 143, or 993 for IMAP over TLS; STARTTLS can encrypt a connection begun on port 143. RFC 9051 defines the current version.

sources.title: RFC 9051: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) - Version 4rev2

title: Post Office Protocol
article: Post Office Protocol

definition.text: POP is an application-layer Internet standard protocol that email clients use to retrieve email from a mail server.

facts.text: POP gives a client application access to a mailbox (maildrop) on a mail server and supports list, retrieve and delete operations on messages.

POP3 clients typically connect, retrieve all messages, store them on the client computer and delete them from the server. This suited users with only temporary dial-up connections who read mail offline.
Clients may leave mail on the server and download only new messages, identified through the UIDL unique-id list command; the unique identifier is permanent for the maildrop.
Messages are retrieved and marked for deletion by message number, and mail marked for deletion is removed from the maildrop only when the client ends the session.
A POP3 server listens on TCP port 110. Encryption is requested with the STLS command, or by connecting to POP3S on port 995 using TLS.
The original POP3 allowed only an unencrypted USER/PASS login. APOP adds a challenge-response using MD5, and SASL methods are supported through the AUTH extension.
The CAPA command lists extension capabilities, but the extension RFC reaffirmed that POP3's role is simple download-and-delete mailbox handling.

title: POP versus IMAP
article: Post Office Protocol#Comparison with IMAP

definition.text: POP downloads mail to one device, whereas IMAP keeps the mailbox on the server so many clients can share it.

facts.text: POP3 moves messages from the server to the client and deletes them there, though it can leave them. IMAP normally leaves all messages on the server and supports both connected and disconnected use.

POP gives a completely static view of the mailbox; the client must reconnect and re-authenticate to see changes. IMAP gives a dynamic view and reports new mail and changes made by other connected clients.
POP treats the mailbox as a single store with no folders and no server-side message state, so two POP clients cannot sync read state. IMAP keeps folders and flags on the server.
IMAP IDLE lets the server tell connected clients about new mail. POP has no such feature, so clients must reconnect periodically to check.
POP retrieves whole messages with RETR, or headers plus some body lines with TOP. IMAP can fetch individual MIME parts, such as text without attachments, and search messages on the server.
POP is a simpler protocol and easier to implement. IMAP remedies many POP shortcomings but adds complexity and keeps mailbox structure on the server, costing far more server resources per mailbox.
A POP UIDL is a string of visible ASCII characters up to 70 characters, while an IMAP UID is a number local to a folder, paired with a UIDVALIDITY value.
Both are the two most prevalent standard retrieval protocols, and webmail providers such as Gmail and Outlook.com support both.

title: Email delivery
article: Email#Operation

definition.text: Email travels from the sender's mail client through submission and transfer servers, found with DNS MX records, to the recipient's mailbox.

facts.text: The sender's mail user agent formats the message and sends it with the submission protocol, a profile of SMTP, to its local mail submission agent.
The submission agent takes the destination from the SMTP envelope, not the message header. The part before @ is the local part, the part after is a domain name it resolves in DNS.
DNS answers with the MX records listing the domain's mail exchange servers, which are MTAs, often run by the recipient's ISP.

The sending server transfers the message by SMTP. The receiving MTA may forward it to other MTAs before the mail delivery agent places it in the recipient's mailbox, from which the recipient's client collects it by POP3 or IMAP.
Domains usually have several mail exchange servers so they can keep accepting mail when the primary is unavailable.

Email favors reliability over speed to cope with unreliable links and busy servers. Overloaded servers, SMTP's many round trips and downtime slow it; mail can be queued and retried for up to five days before a permanent-failure notice.

Accepting a message obliges an MTA to deliver it or send a bounce message back. Open relays that accepted mail for anyone were exploited by spammers, so they are now rare and many MTAs refuse mail from them.
Variations exist: corporate systems use proprietary client protocols and an Internet mail gateway, and users may use webmail instead of a mail client.

title: MIME
article: Email#Message format > Message body > Multipart messages

definition.text: MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) extends the email format to carry non-ASCII text and multimedia attachments.

facts.text: Internet email was designed for 7-bit ASCII. MIME adds character set specifiers and two content transfer encodings: quoted printable for mostly 7-bit text and base64 for arbitrary binary data.
Base64 is widely used for attachments because SMTP in its original form transports only 7-bit ASCII; the attachment is encoded before sending and decoded on receipt.
A MIME message can hold several parts: multipart/mixed for a cover letter and documents, multipart/alternative for the same content in several formats, multipart/related for HTML with its images.
Parts can nest, and the sender can mark a part as shown inline or as an attachment.
A MIME message forms a tree whose leaves are single-part content types and whose inner nodes are multipart types, which lets IMAP fetch one part without the rest.

title: Email attachment size limits
article: Email#Issues > Attachment size limitation

definition.text: Attachments are files appended to an email, and servers cap their size in practice.

facts.text: There is in principle no technical limit on attachments, but clients, servers and ISPs limit file or message size, typically to 25MB or less in the early 2010s.
The size the transport sees can differ from what the user sees, which makes it hard for senders to judge whether a file will go through.
SMTP receivers must accept message content of at least 64K octets, but sizes have grown, so limits should be avoided; servers that impose one should offer the SIZE extension.
Larger files are commonly shared through file hosting services instead.

notes: excluded: protocol detail beyond what the Gmail design needs

title: Email spoofing
article: Email#Issues > Email spoofing

definition.text: Email spoofing is designing a message's header so it appears to come from a known or trusted source.

facts.text: Spam and phishing typically use spoofing to mislead the recipient about the message's true origin.
Spoofing is possible because original SMTP could not authenticate senders, and even casual users can negotiate directly with receiving and relaying servers to build a misleading message.
A sender's own software can set From freely, but a domain owner can specify which servers may send for the domain, and servers can sign mail (SPF and DKIM), so spoofed addresses can be flagged.
These techniques do not protect against misspelled lookalike domain names.

title: MX record
article: MX record

definition.text: An MX record is a DNS resource record naming the mail server responsible for accepting email on behalf of a domain.

facts.text: An MX record carries a preference value and the host name of a mail server. A domain may have one or more of them.
A sending MTA queries DNS for the MX records of each recipient's domain, gets a list of mail servers with preferences, and tries the lowest preference number first.
The preference is an unsigned 16-bit field, so valid values range from 0 to 65535.
The host named in an MX record must map to one or more address records (A or AAAA) and must not point to a CNAME record.

With no MX record, the sender treats the domain as having an implicit MX of preference 0 pointing at itself and looks up its address records. If MX records exist, other address records must not be used.
A nonexistent-domain answer must be reported as an error, while a temporary DNS error means the message must be queued and retried later.
Several MX records, typically pointing to an array of mail servers, give load balancing and redundancy, and allow high-availability clusters of mail gateways for one domain.
MX records cannot move mail service to another port and cannot weight servers of unequal priority.

title: MX failover and load distribution
article: MX record#MX preference, distance, and priority

definition.text: Mail senders spread load and survive server failure by trying MX hosts in preference order and randomizing among equals.

facts.text: Equal preference spreads incoming mail over a set of servers: the sender must randomize among them unless it has a clear reason to favour one, and try all of them before higher numbers.
A multihomed host can instead return several IP addresses, so DNS does the balancing. Senders must follow the returned order, leaving DNS free to use round robin, server load or other schemes.
A sender must try and retry each address in order until delivery succeeds, delaying retries. The RFC does not say whether to retry the same server or a more distant MX, and implementations differ.
Spammers may target a backup, high-distance MX first, assuming weaker filters, and the nolisting anti-spam technique relies on that behaviour.

notes: excluded: protocol detail beyond what the Gmail design needs

title: Email spam
article: Email spam

definition.text: Email spam is unsolicited messages sent in bulk by email.

facts.text: Spam burdens recipients, who must manage, filter or delete it without compensation from the sender, making it a negative externality.
Sending is cheap, so spam grew to an estimated 90% of global email traffic by 2014, and about 85% of email in 2021.
Spammers need recipient addresses, so they and list merchants gather huge lists, harvesting addresses without the owners' consent.
Spammers misspell filtered words or hide the message text in an image to defeat pattern-matching and text-based filters.
Spammers use vulnerable third-party systems such as open mail relays, open proxies and networks of malware-infected PCs (zombies) to send mail.

To resist such abuse, administrators pre-emptively block dynamic IP ranges, require forward-confirmed reverse DNS and impose strict requirements on delivering servers, which can burden small domestic mail servers. Many ISPs block outgoing port 25.

title: Spam filtering
article: Email spam#Anti-spam techniques

definition.text: Spam filtering combines techniques that detect and refuse unsolicited bulk mail.

facts.text: Popular methods are content-based filtering, DNS-based blackhole lists (DNSBL), greylisting, spamtraps, enforcing SMTP's technical requirements, checksumming to detect bulk mail, and costs on the sender such as proof-of-work or micropayments. Each has strengths and weaknesses.
Bayesian filters rely roughly on word probabilities: a message with many words used only in spam and few never used in spam is likely spam. Machine learning more broadly can also identify spam.
Spammers adapt, for example by adding random words to weaken Bayesian filters (Bayesian poisoning), so filtering is an escalating game against new evasion techniques.
Outbound spam protection applies the same techniques to mail leaving a provider's network and blocks the message or shuts off its source.
Email authentication against forged From addresses became popular in the 2010s. Servers use SPF, DKIM and DMARC, DNSBLs and greylisting to reject or quarantine suspicious mail.

Filtering has collateral damage: it uses server and network resources, rejected legitimate mail forces senders to contact recipients out of channel, and mail sent to a spam folder gives the sender no notice.
Silently dropping mail violates the expectation that mail is delivered or returned, so it should be considered only with very high confidence that a message is seriously fraudulent.
IMAP defines $Junk and $NotJunk keywords so users or delivery agents can mark junk, and $Phishing for likely phishing mail, which should also be filed as junk.

sources.title: RFC 9051: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) - Version 4rev2

title: SMTP mail transaction
article: rfc>5321#3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions

definition.text: An SMTP mail transaction hands one message to a server in three steps: MAIL, one or more RCPT, then DATA.

facts.text: A session starts when the client opens a connection and the server sends a greeting; the client then normally sends EHLO to identify itself. The dialog is deliberately lock-step, one command at a time, unless pipelining is agreed.
MAIL starts a transaction and resets the receiver's state. Its reverse-path is the source mailbox used to report errors, and a 250 reply accepts it.
RCPT gives one forward-path per command and can be repeated. A recipient known to be undeliverable gets a 550 reply, and RCPT without a prior MAIL gets 503.
After DATA the server replies 354 and treats the following lines as the message until a line holding only a period. The client must not send message data unless it gets 354.
To let users send a line that is a single period, the client adds an extra leading period to any line starting with one and the server removes it.

When the server finishes storing the data it sends 250, which confirms the transaction. By returning 2yz it accepts responsibility to deliver the message, retry transient failures and notify the sender of permanent ones.
A 4yz after the end of data means the server must not deliver, and the client keeps responsibility and may requeue. A 5yz means the client should not retry to the same server without review.
The client ends the connection with QUIT, to which the receiver must send a 221 reply before closing the channel.

title: SMTP reply codes
article: rfc>5321#4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.2. SMTP Replies > 4.2.1. Reply Code Severities and Theory

definition.text: Every SMTP reply starts with a three-digit code whose first digit says whether the command succeeded, needs more, or failed temporarily or permanently.

facts.text: The first digit gives the class: 2yz positive completion, 3yz positive intermediate (more input expected, as in DATA), 4yz transient negative and 5yz permanent negative.
A reply is 4yz if repeating the identical command could succeed later, and the client should try again; for a 5yz the client should not repeat the exact request.

The second digit gives a category such as syntax, information, connections or mail system, and the third a finer gradation. Reply text is recommended but the codes must follow the specification strictly.
A multiline reply puts a hyphen after the code on every line but the last, and all lines carry the same code.

notes: excluded: protocol detail beyond what the Gmail design needs

title: SMTP queueing and retries
article: rfc>5321#4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy

definition.text: An SMTP sender keeps mail that cannot be sent at once in a queue and retries it periodically until it succeeds or gives up.

facts.text: Mail that cannot be transmitted immediately must be queued and periodically retried, and a queue entry holds the envelope information as well as the message.
After a failed attempt the sender must delay retrying that destination. The retry interval should be at least 30 minutes, and the give-up time generally needs to be at least 4-5 days.
Failures are typically transient, which favors two connection attempts in the first hour in the queue and then backing off to one every two or three hours.
A client should keep a list of unreachable hosts with their timeouts rather than retry every queued item, because retrying many messages to a dead host wastes Internet overhead and blocks the sender.
When several recipients share a destination server only one copy should be sent: one MAIL, a RCPT for each recipient, then one DATA.
A client may run several concurrent outgoing transactions for timely delivery, with a limit to protect the host, and a server should accept more than one incoming transaction at a time.
Receiving mail from a host suggests that mail queued for it can now be sent, which can remove the need for an explicit send-queue command.
Retry parameters must be configurable and every activity must have a per-command timeout. A receiver must answer the end-of-data promptly to avoid duplicates after timeouts.

title: Bounce messages
article: rfc>5321#6. Problem Detection and Handling > 6.1. Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email

definition.text: A bounce message is the notice an SMTP server sends the originator when it accepted a message but cannot deliver it.

facts.text: A server that accepts a message with 250 after DATA accepts responsibility for delivering or relaying it, and must not lose it for frivolous reasons such as a later host crash.

If delivery fails after acceptance, the server must send a notification to the envelope return path, using a null reverse-path <> for the notice; no notification is sent when the return path is already null.
Servers must not send notifications about problems with notifications; the null reverse-path prevents error-report loops.
Some failures after acceptance cannot be avoided, for example when a soft DNS error blocks recipient validation, the target is a mailing list, or the server is a relay.
Rejecting a message during the SMTP transaction is better than bouncing it afterwards. Servers that check recipients only after receiving the text cannot tell the client which recipient failed.
Backscatter happens when a misconfigured server bounces mail whose envelope sender was forged, so the bounce lands on an innocent party; many ISPs disable non-delivery reports for this reason.
Servers should avoid sending bounces for mail judged hostile unless confident that the bounce will be usefully delivered.

title: SMTP envelope versus message header
article: rfc>5321#2. The SMTP Model > 2.3. SMTP Terminology > 2.3.1. Mail Objects

definition.text: A mail object has an envelope that SMTP uses for delivery and content made of a header section and a body.

facts.text: The envelope holds an originator address to which errors are reported, one or more recipient addresses and optional extension data. The content, sent in DATA, has a header section and a body.

Delivery follows the envelope, not the header: the To field may be unrelated to the addresses the message is delivered to, as the letter's address differs from the outer envelope, and From may not be the actual sender.
Bcc recipients are normally given only in the SMTP envelope and not listed in the message header.
Return-Path, added at final delivery, preserves the MAIL command's reverse-path, which can differ from the sender's mailbox when errors go to a special error-handling mailbox.
The content is US-ASCII text and header fields are always US-ASCII, though extensions such as 8BITMIME can relax the restriction for the body.

title: Mailing lists and aliases
article: rfc>5321#3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.9. Mailing Lists and Aliases

definition.text: A mailing list or alias is a pseudo-mailbox that SMTP expands into a list of destination mailboxes.

facts.text: Multi-destination delivery transforms a pseudo-mailbox address into a list of mailbox addresses, called an alias or a list depending on the expansion rules, and a host should support both.
To expand an alias, the mailer replaces the pseudo-mailbox in the envelope with each expanded address and leaves the rest of the envelope and the body unchanged.

A list redistributes rather than forwards: the envelope return address becomes the list administrator, so delivery errors go to the administrator and not to the originator, while the header From stays unchanged.
A list that makes extensive changes to a message and envelope must be treated as a full user agent, which accepts a delivery and posts a new message.

notes: excluded: protocol detail beyond what the Gmail design needs

definition.text: An Internet email message is a header section of fields followed by an optional body, in the syntax RFC 5322 specifies.

facts.text: A message consists of header fields, optionally followed by a body, with the header separated from the body by a blank line. RFC 5322 defines the syntax and MIME extends it.
A header field is a name, a colon and a field body. Long field bodies can be folded onto several lines by inserting a line break before whitespace and unfolded by removing it.
A conformant message uses US-ASCII characters. Each line must be at most 998 characters and should be at most 78, excluding the CRLF.
The header fields carry most of the semantic information; for RFC 5322 the body is a series of uninterpreted lines of text, and MIME defines other body structures.
Non-ASCII header text uses the RFC 2047 encoded-word syntax, and non-ASCII bodies use MIME encodings. UTF-8 in headers and addresses needs the newer internationalization extensions.
A message header must include at least a From field and a Date field.

title: Email header fields
article: rfc>5322#3. Syntax > 3.6. Field Definitions

definition.text: Email header fields fall into groups: originator, destination, identification, informational, trace and resent fields.

facts.text: From names the author, Sender names the agent that actually transmitted the message and must appear when From has several mailboxes, and Reply-To suggests where replies go. Without it, replies go to From.
To holds the primary recipients, Cc others who receive a copy, and Bcc recipients whose addresses are not revealed to the other recipients.
How Bcc is handled is implementation dependent: the Bcc line may be removed from every copy, or Bcc recipients may get a separate copy that carries it.
Every message should have a Message-ID, and replies should carry In-Reply-To and References fields.
Subject, Comments and Keywords are optional fields meant for human-readable information about the message; Subject is the most common and gives a short topic.
Each SMTP server prepends a Received trace line and must not change or delete earlier ones, and the final delivery adds Return-Path. The timestamps help find slow relays.
Servers can record authentication checks in header fields such as Authentication-Results, Received-SPF and DKIM-Signature for downstream agents.
Resent fields are added when a user reintroduces a message into the transport system; they are informational and must not drive normal reply handling.

title: Message-ID and email threading
article: rfc>5322#3. Syntax > 3.6. Field Definitions > 3.6.4. Identification Fields

definition.text: A Message-ID is a globally unique identifier for one version of a message, and replies use it to link messages into threads.

facts.text: The Message-ID holds a single machine-readable identifier of one version of a message. The generating host must guarantee it is globally unique; a revised message gets a new one.
A good method is to put the host's domain name on the right of the @ and a combination of the current date and time and a unique value, such as a process id, on the left.
A reply's In-Reply-To holds its parent's Message-ID, while References holds the parent's References followed by the parent's Message-ID, identifying a conversation thread.
Some clients walk back through References to rebuild a thread, assuming each message has one parent, so building References for a reply with several parents is discouraged.

notes: excluded: protocol detail beyond what the Gmail design needs

title: Email address
article: rfc>5322#3. Syntax > 3.4. Address Specification > 3.4.1. Addr-Spec Specification

definition.text: An email address is a locally interpreted string, an at-sign and an Internet domain.

facts.text: The domain says where mail is delivered, as a domain name or an IP address literal. The local part is a domain-dependent string the host reads as a mailbox name.
The local part uses the dot-atom form when it can; the quoted-string form is used only for characters a dot-atom cannot hold.
SMTP caps a local part at 64 octets, a domain at 255 octets and a path at 256 octets.

title: IMAP unique identifiers
article: rfc>9051#2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers > 2.3.1.1. Unique Identifier (UID) Message Attribute

definition.text: An IMAP unique identifier (UID) is a number that identifies a message in a mailbox, stable across sessions when paired with the mailbox's UIDVALIDITY.

facts.text: IMAP addresses a message by its UID or by its message sequence number, which is its relative position from 1 to the number of messages in the mailbox.
A UID is an unsigned non-zero 32-bit value assigned in strictly ascending order as messages are added; UIDs need not be contiguous, unlike sequence numbers.
A UID must not change during a session and should not change between sessions. Persistent UIDs let a client resynchronize its state, for example an offline client.
UIDVALIDITY lets a client detect changed UIDs: if UIDs fail to persist, the new value must be greater than the old, and a 32-bit date-time or a global counter makes a good value.
UIDNEXT is the predicted UID of the next new message. It changes whenever messages are added, even if later expunged, so a client can tell whether mail arrived since it last checked.
The mailbox name, UIDVALIDITY and UID together must refer to a single immutable message forever, and an expunged message's UID is never reused under the same UIDVALIDITY.

title: IMAP message flags
article: rfc>9051#2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.2. Flags Message Attribute

definition.text: IMAP flags are named tokens attached to a message on the server that record its state, such as read or deleted.

facts.text: A flag is set by adding it to the message's list and cleared by removing it. System flags are predefined and start with a backslash; keywords are defined by the server and do not.
The system flags are \Seen (read), \Answered, \Flagged (urgent), \Deleted (to be removed by a later EXPUNGE) and \Draft.
Defined keywords include $Forwarded, $Junk and $NotJunk, which are mutually exclusive, and $Phishing, which a delivery agent sets for probable phishing mail.
A flag is permanent or session-only: changes to permanent flags are seen by concurrent and later sessions, while session flags last only for that session.

title: IMAP IDLE
article: rfc>9051#6. Client Commands > 6.3. Client Commands - Authenticated State > 6.3.13. IDLE Command

definition.text: IMAP IDLE lets a client ask the server to push mailbox changes in real time instead of polling.

facts.text: Without IDLE a client would have to poll the server for new mail, deletions and flag changes. IDLE lets the server send updates in real time so the user sees new mail at once.
The server answers IDLE with a continuation response. While it is active the server may send untagged EXISTS, EXPUNGE and FETCH responses at any time, until the client sends DONE.
A client must not send another command while the server awaits DONE, because the server could not tell the command from the continuation.

A server may treat an idling client as inactive and log it off after its timeout, so clients should end and reissue IDLE at least every 29 minutes; a post-authentication autologout timer must last at least 30 minutes.

title: IMAP commands and responses
article: rfc>9051#2. Protocol Overview > 2.2. Commands and Responses

definition.text: An IMAP session is a text dialogue in which the client sends tagged commands and the server returns data and a tagged completion result.

facts.text: IMAP assumes a reliable data stream such as TCP and listens on port 143, or 993 for implicit TLS. Everything is sent as lines ending in CRLF.
Each client command carries a tag, and the server's completion response repeats it with OK, NO or BAD (protocol error), so the tag shows which command finished when several are in progress.

Server data and non-completion status are prefixed with "*" as untagged responses, and may be sent unilaterally. A client must be ready to accept any response at any time and should cache server data.
A client may pipeline commands without waiting for completion, but if a command could affect another's results the server must execute them in the order given.
The server must send mailbox size updates automatically and should send flag updates; only EXPUNGE may reduce the message count, because EXISTS cannot.

A connection is in one of four states, not authenticated, authenticated, selected or logout; most commands are valid in only some states, and a client must select a mailbox before commands that affect messages.

title: IMAP search and fetch
article: rfc>9051#6. Client Commands > 6.4. Client Commands - Selected State > 6.4.4. SEARCH Command

definition.text: IMAP SEARCH makes the server find messages by criteria and FETCH retrieves chosen parts of them.

facts.text: SEARCH matches messages on the server against criteria, and several keys are combined with AND. Result options return the lowest (MIN), highest (MAX), all (ALL) or the count (COUNT) of matching messages.
FETCH retrieves message data such as FLAGS, ENVELOPE, BODYSTRUCTURE or RFC822.SIZE, with macros ALL, FAST and FULL for common sets of items.
A client can fetch the header, the body, one body part, or a byte range of any of them, so it can load text without attachments; BODY.PEEK does not set the \Seen flag.
SEARCH servers must support US-ASCII and UTF-8 charsets and decode content transfer encodings and header text before comparing.
